en: Ratnākaraśānti: The Hevajra Sādhana titled *Bhramahara* (Dispeller of Delusion) (BhrHe 157)
With faces resembling the clouds at the time of universal dissolution, emitting roars as they shook the oceans by the force of their footsteps upon the earth,
they caused the mountain peaks to collapse under the wind from their forest-like arms.
May this terrifying *tāṇḍava* dance of Heruka be for your protection.
I shall compose the *sādhana* for the eight-faced Hevajra, who has three eyes on each face,
who moves with four legs, and possesses sixteen arms.

Here, the practitioner engaged in cultivation, having risen in the morning, having placed his own seed-syllable upon the sun at the heart, and having performed the purification of the mouth and other rites, should perform the protection of the site and himself with the mantra:
*oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Then, entering the meditation ground made fragrant with perfumes, flowers, and the like, he should proceed.
Having assumed the cross-legged posture on a comfortable seat and having consecrated the water for the guest-offering (*argha*) with recitation,
one should gaze upon the Blessed One together with his retinue in the sky before oneself, drawn there by the rays of light from the heart-mantra.
One should worship with the eight goddesses, Gaurī and the others, who have emerged from the seed-syllable in the heart. Among them, Gaurī bears the Moon, Caurī the Sun,
and Vettālī Water.
Ghasmarī is meat, Pukkasī is sandalwood,
and Śabarī is honey.
The Caṇḍālī plays the hand-drum, and the Ḍombī, clinging to his neck, acts as a man. Then, in the presence of that very Blessed One, one should perform the confession of sins and so forth.
(BhrHe 158)
I confess all my own misdeeds before the Blessed One;
I rejoice in all the roots of merit of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble ones, and ordinary beings;
and I dedicate all my own roots of merit toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Thus, until I reach enlightenment...

I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Blessed One, the foremost among two-legged beings. I go for refuge to the Dharma, the complete Mahāyāna. I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the assembly of irreversible bodhisattvas. Oh, may I indeed awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings, until—
For the sake of establishing [beings] in ultimate Nirvana and in the enlightenment of a Buddha, I take recourse in this unsurpassed path to enlightenment,
namely, the Vajrayāna.
Thereafter, [one should cultivate] loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, which takes the form of bestowing divine happiness.

One should cultivate compassion in the form of removing all suffering, sympathetic joy in the form of the certainty of never being separated from divine bliss, and equanimity in the form of providing the path that is the antidote to the afflictions. Then, having taken all phenomena as objects with the mind, one should investigate: "This is merely the mind, deluded by this or that aspect."
It appears just as in a dream.

There is nothing external to the mind that can be grasped by the mind. Because there is no object of grasp, the mind itself does not become a grasper. Therefore, all phenomena have the mind as their essence.

The emptiness of the grasped and the grasper is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Having thus determined this with absolute certainty, one should abandon the forms of all phenomena—which are superimposed by delusion and are the marks of delusion—and perceive their very nature alone, characterized as non-dual cognition, resembling pure crystal, like the stainless autumn sky at midday, infinite. This is called...
Ultimate bodhicitta is supramundane gnosis of emptiness, free from conceptual proliferation and non-conceptual.
Therefore, one should empower it with the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.

That very Blessed Prajñāpāramitā is itself the supreme protection. Therefore, one should meditate upon the formalized protection that is its natural outflow, which has the nature of pure mundane knowledge.
Having visualized the sun in front by means of the syllable *repha*, one should visualize a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) arising from *hūṃ* within that sun;
and by means of that very vajra, one should visualize a rampart and the binding of a cage.

Having radiated everywhere with universal vajra-rays, which are as unbearable as the fire of cosmic destruction, and having condensed them, one fashions a blazing vajra-fortress, square and horizontal,
and above it, a vajra-canopy.

One should visualize below a ground made of vajra, extending down to the bottom of the netherworld (rasātala). Then, by means of the sun and the universal vajra, they become rays of light that radiate out in every direction; having condensed, one should establish the boundary-binding (sīmābandha) far outside.
This is the meaning of the verse.
Thereafter, one should contemplate the five purified great elements as the very outflow of that [vajra-ground]. Among them, the great element of space—

That which is called the *dharmodayā* has the nature of Mahāvajradhara; it is white as the autumnal moon, narrow at the bottom and wide at the top, triangular, and its interior has the nature of space. Within it stands a vast *viśvavajra* upon the pericarp of a universal lotus (*viśvadala-kamala*) that has emerged from the inside. Upon its pedestal are the four great elements, in the form of four mandalas, having the nature of the four goddesses, situated one above the other.
One should visualize as follows: first, by means of the syllable *laṃ*, the mandala of Mahendra, which is square, yellow, and marked with three-pronged vajras at its corners.

Then, by means of the syllable *vaṃ*, the mandala of Varuṇa, which is circular, white, and marked with a water-jar. Then, by means of the syllable *raṃ*, the mandala of Agni, which is triangular, red, and marked with the letter *ra* at its corners. Then, by means of the syllable *yaṃ*, the mandala of Vāyu, which is shaped like a bow, black, and marked with fluttering banners at both ends.

At that time, however, the practitioner [should consider] that very supramundane gnosis (*lokottarajñāna*) as abiding as the all-pervading [reality]. Thereupon, in the center of the universal vajra-vedikā, he should meditate upon a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) made of various jewels, which is the nature of Vairocana and constitutes the Great City of Liberation— the condensed form of the utterly pure buddha-field— born from the transformation of the four great elements, and surrounded by eight cremation grounds that indicate the selflessness of all world-systems.
It is square, with four gates, adorned with eight pillars,
surrounded by four altars, and embellished with four archways.
It is beautiful with necklaces, half-necklaces, ribbons, garlands, canopies, mirrors, and chowries; and it radiates a flood of Buddhas through vajra-threads and rays of light.
The quarters of the sky were made resonant by the bells at the tips of fluttering silken banners,
and there was great joy through the five supreme objects of desire and various offerings.
Within its womb-chamber is an eight-petalled lotus with filaments;
on the four doors, the four corners, and the pericarp are the seats.
Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and Rudra, as well as Yama, the Lord of Yakṣas, Nairṛti, and Vemacitrin; and in the center, the fourfold Māras.
Each subsequent member of the fourfold host of Māra was more exposed and terrified than the last;
their hearts were overwhelmed by the sun, while others were even more cowardly than the moon.

There, upon the central seat, is a moon mandala consisting of the fifteen vowels, which has the nature of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); above that is a sun mandala consisting of the thirty-four consonants, which has the nature of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*);
in the center of that, from the transformation of the syllables *aṃ* and *hūṃ*, [arises the seed-syllable].

One should contemplate the *kartti* (knife) and *kapāla* (skull-cup) joined together, situated within one's own seed-syllable (*bīja*), and consisting of the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Then, having emanated all the Tathāgatas from the two seed-syllables in the form of a circle of yoginīs,
and having withdrawn them,
the seed-syllable unified with them is the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).

Then, one should visualize the Blessed Lord Vajrasattva, born from the transformation of the seed-syllables marked by the moon and sun, manifested in the form of Śrī Heruka with the colors, shapes, and symbols to be described hereafter, likewise embraced at the neck by Nairātmyā, and consisting of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu-jñāna*.
This is the awakening through the five aspects (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*).
From the mouth of that blissful one, the two blazing seed-syllables, interlaced with two *huṃ* syllables,
enter within the lotus out of passion and melt.
Then the Vajrin, having melted through great passion together with the Vidyā,
should remain in the state of the maṇḍala, resembling the flow of the autumn moon.
Then, for the purpose of his rising, the goddesses, stationed upon the moon-seats at the corners,
should urge him with four vajra-songs.
Arise, O Bharaṭa! With a compassionate mind, cry out for me and protect me!
Abandon me, O Kāma, and [abandon] that void-meditation which is devoid of the union with Great Bliss.
Even when you have departed, I shall die; arise, O Hevajra!
Abandon this nature of emptiness; let the task of the Śavarī be accomplished.
Having invited the world, O Lord of the Gods, why do you remain in emptiness?
Haṃ! I am a Caṇḍālī; without you, I do not appear even in my dreams.
O Indīālī, arise! I know your heart; we are *ḍombīs*, so do not harbor a mind of pity or compassion.

Then, in accordance with the *gītikā*, having ascertained that the symbols, bodies, and so forth of the deities— arising from the syllables *Aṃ* and *Hūṃ* produced by the melting and gathering of the moon, which reside within the solar mandala of that moment— are like space and like an illusion,
one should [visualize] that very same thing within the womb of the joined *kartī* (knife) and skull-cup, which are the nature of firm meditative concentration (*dṛḍhasamādhi*).

One should perceive the two seed-syllables as having the nature of the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*). Then, by means of the yoga of emanation (*spharaṇa*), one should discern the universe as consisting of the infinite Tathāgatas in the form of the circle of Yoginīs and as being dependent upon the mind.

By means of the yoga of reabsorption (*saṃharaṇa*), having thoroughly understood that everything is like an illusion and like space, one should perceive oneself as the glorious Heruka, born from the transformation of the second seed-syllable marked with a sun.
He was stamping his feet and threatening the gods and asuras;
he was enraged with round, red eyes, yet graceful and in the bloom of youth.
He has four legs, eight faces, and is adorned with sixteen arms;
he stands in the *ardhaparyaṅka* posture, performing a dance while treading upon the four Māras.
Wearing a great necklace of severed heads, he stands upon the sun, terrifying and formidable;
holding a universal vajra upon his head, he is black in color with a radiance blazing like the sun.
His face is expanded by the syllable HŪṂ, his body is smeared with ashes;
his primary face is intensely black, while the right is white like a kunda flower.
The left face is red, most terrible, and distorted with a gaping mouth;
all the remaining faces are like the color of bees, and each face has three eyes.
It is endowed with the nine dramatic sentiments (nāṭyarasa): the erotic, the heroic, the loathsome, the furious, the comic, the terrifying, the pathetic, the marvelous, and the tranquil.
His hair and eyelashes are tawny and upright; he is adorned with the five insignia:
the discus, the earrings, the necklace, the bracelet on the hand, and the girdle.
Likewise, the elephant, horse, donkey, cow, camel, human, śarabha,
and otter are to be known as being on the eight southern skull-bowls in successive order.
Earth, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Fire, the Moon, the Sun, Antaka, and Dhanada— these are the guardians of its eight quarters.
Having entered the meditative absorption of selflessness, she possesses her own fivefold mudrā;
she has two arms, one face, and two legs, and she holds a curved knife and a skull-cup.
Then, one should contemplate the syllable *hūṃ* in the sun-disk of the skull situated upon the sun at the heart of the Blessed One,

and the syllable *aṃ* in the moon-disk of the hand-gesture (karttimuṣṭi) situated upon the moon at the heart of the Blessed Lady. Then, one should contemplate Nairātmyā in his ear and Vajrā in his eye.
In the nose is Guhyagaurī; in the tongue is Vāriyoginī;
in the faculty of the body is Vajraḍākī.
One should resolve upon selflessness in the mind. This very pentad of Vajra and so forth corresponds respectively to the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

likewise, to delusion, stinginess, passion, envy, and hatred. In the sense-bases of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena, there are the external Gaurī, Caurī, Vettālī, Ghasmarī, Bhūcarī, and Khecarī.
In the elements of earth, water, fire, and air, there are Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī.
Within body, speech, and mind reside Bhūcarī, Khecarī, and Nairātmyā;
in the flesh is Pukkasī,
and in the blood is Śabarī.
In the semen is Caṇḍālī; in the marrow and fat is Ḍombī;
and in the skin are the seven factors of enlightenment.
The four truths reside in the bones. Having thus performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) by means of the deities, one should resolve upon the other purifications:

through compassion, the eyes are red; through a mind of loving-kindness, the body is black; the feet are the articles of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); and the sixteen arms are the sixteen emptinesses (*śūnyatā*).
The eight faces are the eight liberations; he has three eyes because of the three realities; the five seals are the five Jinas; and in his wrath, he disciplines the wicked.
The four wheels located respectively in the throat, heart, genitals, and crown are known as the Enjoyment, Dharma, Emanation, and Great Bliss wheels. (BhrHe 167)
There is a lotus with sixteen, eight, sixty-four, and thirty-two petals,
adorned in the center with the forms of the syllables Oṃ, Hūṃ, Āḥ, and Haṃ.

Thereafter, having drawn in the Tathāgatas residing in the ten directions by means of the hooks of light rays radiating from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart and established them in the sky, and having worshipped them with the eight Mothers, one should pray: "May all the Tathāgatas confer empowerment upon me! He is then empowered by them, who have assumed the form of Śrī Heruka and consist of the five Tathāgatas holding vases filled with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). As he is being empowered, Lord Akṣobhya [appears] upon his head.
A rain of flowers and a rain of saffron occurs,
the sound of drums is heard,
and one is worshipped by Rūpavajrā and the others.
He is praised by Locanā and the others with the vajra song.
This is the meditative absorption (samādhi) called Ādiyoga,
and it is the Svābhāvikakāya.
Now, the consecration of the lotus: Oṃ, O Lotus, support of bliss, great passion, giver of bliss!
O Universal One, partaker of the four joys, hūṃ hūṃ, perform my task!
(BhrHe 168) Now, the empowerment of the vajra:
Oṃ vajra, great hatred, bestower of the four joys!
O Lord, whose singular essence is the mouth of the sky-goer, Hūṃ Hūṃ! Accomplish my purpose.
Then,

one should begin the ritual union with "Oṃ śī 3 ha 3 svāhā. Then, [one should visualize the consort] as produced from the syllable Gaṃ, which arises from the transformation of drops of lunar fluid fallen into the interior of a lotus.

One should visualize Gaurī, who is black in color and holds a dagger and a blood-filled vessel, upon the moon of the seat at the eastern gate. Likewise, by means of the syllable Caṃ, one should visualize Caurī, who is madder-red in color and holds a fire-pit and a boar, upon the moon of the seat at the southern gate.
Likewise, by means of the syllable Vaṃ, one should visualize Vettālī, who is golden in color and holds a tortoise and a skull-cup, upon the moon of the seat at the western gate.

Likewise, by means of the syllable *ghaṃ*, one visualizes Ghasmarī, red in color, holding a snake and a yogapaṭṭra vessel, upon the moon at the seat of the northern gate; likewise, by means of the syllable *paṃ*, Pukkasī, resembling a sapphire, holding a lion and a sword, upon the moon at the seat of the northeastern corner; likewise, by means of the syllable *śaṃ*, Śabarī, resembling a moonstone, holding a mendicant’s bowl and a small water-pot, upon the moon at the seat of the southeastern corner. (BhrHe 169)
Likewise, with the syllable *laṃ*, one should meditate on Caṇḍālī, who is sky-blue in color, holding a wheel and a plow, upon the moon-seat in the southwest corner;
likewise, with the syllable *ḍaṃ*, one should meditate on Ḍombī, who is variegated in color, holding a vajra and a threatening gesture (tarjanī), upon the moon-seat in the northwest corner.
They stand in the half-lotus dance posture (*ardhaparyaṅka-nāṭya*), are circular, red, and have three eyes.
They have tawny hair standing upright, two arms, and they wear the five mudrās.
Then, having surveyed the mandala completed all around, one should draw in the wisdom-mandala with the hooks of light rays from the seed-syllable in the heart;
having stationed it in the sky facing the eastern gate,
one should dispel obstacles with the eight-faced *hūṃ* syllables.
Having offered the *argha* and *pādya*,
one should perform the rites of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), entering (*praveśana*), binding (*bandhana*), and subduing (*vaśīkaraṇa*) respectively with the syllables *jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *hoḥ*.

Having meditated on the state of the single fusion between the *samaya* and the *jñāna* maṇḍalas, one should attract all the Tathāgatas with rays from the heart-mantra, worship them, and entreat them to bestow the consecration upon those two. As they are being consecrated, the Conqueror of the Consecration arises upon their heads. Regarding this, there are two verses:
"The four [consorts] beginning with Pukkasī and the four beginning with Gaurī [are to be placed] in due order..."
One should seal this here with Akṣobhya, Ratneśa, and Vāgīśa.
The Herukas of existence and nirvāṇa [are worshipped] by the lords of their families, [namely] body, speech, and mind;
while Vajra and the others are [worshipped] by the lords of their own families, the Jinas, the five Akṣobhyas.
Then, one should bring to mind the reality (*tattva*) of the deities. Here, all phenomena (*dharmas*) are subsumed within body, speech, mind, and gnosis.

The reality of the gatekeepers consists in the discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇa*), as appropriate, of the true nature (*dharmatā*) of those [four]—body and so forth—which is representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) and the emptiness of duality (*dvayaśūnyatā*). The correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) of that very emptiness is non-conceptual (*niṣprapañca*) and untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*).

The unsurpassed Vajrayāna is the reality (*tattva*) of the four [classes], such as the *pukkasī* and others, according to their respective yogas. The fruit of that very Vajrayāna is the state of the Great Vajradhara, the unsurpassed awakening, which is the reality of the Lord of the Maṇḍala.

Then, having emanated the eight offering goddesses from the seed-syllable at one's own heart, and having filled the sky with clouds of their emanations, one should worship the maṇḍala together with its presiding deity. Thereafter, one should resolve that all phenomena are like an illusion.
One should praise the Blessed One with two verses:
"Having delighted him with various and manifold glances full of playful charm, and having delighted him with various and manifold kisses and embraces..."
Having partaken of various and manifold foods that provide pleasure,
and having consumed the various and manifold vows, oh, manifest yourself!
Let him practice equanimity toward all women;
let the whole world eat all kinds of food.
Then, having visualized a vajra in the intermediate space with the syllable *hūṃ*,
below it a lotus with the syllable *āḥ*,
and in its center the ritual substances marked with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*).
From the union of the vajra and the lotus, there is the blazing of fire; by that, their heating occurs;
through cooking, they are liquefied, and by being transformed into the sun of gnosis, they are illuminated.
By those rays, one should behold the forms of all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions;

having drawn forth the nectar of gnosis from the seeds of their gnosis by means of those very rays and poured it into them, one should make them of one flavor (*samarasī-kuryāt*). Having thus rendered them into nectar and empowered them with the three syllables, one should visualize a mandala upon the tongue and the sun at the heart by means of the syllable *HŪṂ*.
With those nectars, one should satisfy oneself and the mandala.
Within the delightful city of the circle of Mothers (mātṛcakra), one should contemplate the Lord in this way:
as one who has attained waveless bliss and whose very nature is waveless.
Thus ends the second meditative absorption, named "The Supreme King of Mandalas," which is the Enjoyment Body (*sāṃbhogika-kāya*).
Then, having emanated Gaurī, Caurī, and so forth, up to the Lord of the Mandala, one by one in succession and without interval throughout the ten directions,
and having performed the benefit of sentient beings,
one reabsorbs them back into those very [deities].

One should visualize the mandala and the lord of the mandala as having accomplished their task and being absorbed in the bliss of non-conceptualization (*niṣprapañcasukha*). In that regard, Gaurī establishes sentient beings through the correct analytical observation of the body;
Caurī, of the mind;
and Vettālī, of speech.
Ghasmarī is the gnosis of wisdom, Pukkasī is the body of correct knowledge,
and Śabarī is the mind.
Caṇḍālī is the speech, and Ḍombī is the gnosis. The Lord of the Maṇḍala, however, establishes sentient beings in the state of Mahāvajradhara.
Immediately thereafter, one should meditate on equanimity through the yoga of the six limbs.
One should meditate upon the wheel together with its presiding deity, in sequence as black, red, yellow, green, blue, and white, and finally as consisting solely of innate bliss (sahajānanda).
Thus is the third meditative stabilization called Karmarājāgra,
and the emanation body (*nairmāṇikakāya*). One who is weary from meditation should recite the mantra, having visualized oneself as the maṇḍala manifested in the form of the deity.

"Oṃ deva picuvajra hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā. Having mentally inscribed these thirteen mantra-syllables—upright-headed and blazing like lamps—within the solar disc at the heart as a single mandala, one should recite them with the vajra-voice or the wrathful voice while uttering them. [They emerge] from all mouths and from the mouths of all goddesses.
One should resolve that one is reciting the mantra. By this alone, the eightfold recitation of one's own deity and the mantra-recitation of all goddesses is accomplished.
Then, one should make a formal aspiration (praṇidhāna).

Through these roots of merit, may I attain the state of the Great Vajra-Holder, which is the all-encompassing essence of all Buddhas; and through them, may I cause the entire world to attain that same state.
The conduct for the sake of awakening, and furthermore that which was praised by the Perfectly Awakened Ones by Bodhivajra— may that twofold conduct be mine.
Then, having worshipped the maṇḍala together with its leader as before,
and having internalized the goddesses within the mantra of one's own heart, one should resolve upon the foundation maṇḍala as being exceedingly vast. (BhrHe 174)

Having ascertained that the four great elements are of the nature of the *pukkasa* and other [castes], one should arise with the pride of Hevajra and abide in that very state. At midday and at the evening twilight, having entered the meditation chamber, one should— as before— visualize the foundational maṇḍala and, upon the seat in its center, instantly perceive oneself in the form of the eight-faced Hevajra who has attained meditative absorption (*samāpanna*).
Having emanated the goddesses from the seed-syllable in the heart and seated them in their respective places,
and having meditated upon the entire maṇḍala as consisting of bliss,
one should perform worship, praise, the tasting of nectar, recitation, and so forth. At the time of sleep, [one should practice] the yoga of the six limbs and the yoga of innate bliss.

Having brought [the deity] face-to-face, one should sleep. Awakened by the songs of the four goddesses, one should rise from sleep. Having risen, one should perform everything as before. In this manner, day after day, until one perceives the signs of accomplishment. Having perceived them, one should practice the means for the desired accomplishment according to the tantra.
Having clearly explained the practice of the eight-faced Heruka— the abode of the wealth of the Guru’s qualities— which dispels delusion;
(BhrHe 175)

This merit has been acquired by me, who possesses this birth; by means of that, which is the cause of boundless benefit for those sharing in existence, may I become the Victorious One, the Wielder of the Thunderbolt.
